name: Aztec Empire
summary: The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, which dominated central Mexico until the Spanish conquest.

location.value: Central Mexico, around the Valley of Mexico, extending to the Gulf and Pacific coasts and Soconusco near Guatemala.

terrain.value: The highland Valley of Mexico with Lake Texcoco, where the island-city of Tenochtitlan stood.

climate.value: Highland climate. A severe drought and famine struck in 1450–1454.

resources.value: Maize from chinampas (floating gardens), and tribute of cotton, cacao, feathers and gold.

disasters.value: The famine of 1450–1454, and the smallpox epidemic of 1520, which killed a large share of the population.

population.value: About 6 million in the early 16th century (Wikipedia infobox).

urbanisation.value: Tenochtitlan (founded 1325) was one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps 200,000 people.

disease.value: Smallpox, brought by the Spanish expedition, devastated the population in 1520 and after.

migration.value: The Mexica migrated into the Valley of Mexico around 1250.

economicBase.value: Intensive farming (chinampas), markets (Tlatelolco), and tribute from conquered city-states.

tradeRoutes.value: Long-distance trade by pochteca merchants, who also acted as diplomats and spies.

moneyAndTax.value: Cotton cloth (quachtli) and cacao beans as money. Tribute was paid twice a year by subject cities.

inequality.value: Nobles (pipiltin) were exempt from tribute, which commoners (macehualtin) paid. There were also slaves.

governmentType.value: A hegemonic confederation, the Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, ruling largely indirectly through tribute.

keyRulers.value: Itzcoatl (1427–1440, founder of the alliance). Moctezuma I (1440–1468). Ahuitzotl (1486–1502). Moctezuma II (1502–1520). Cuauhtémoc (1520–1521, last).

succession.value: Rulers (huey tlatoani) were chosen by a council from the royal family.

institutions.value: Schools for nobles and commoners (calmecac and telpochcalli), and law codes under Moctezuma I.

stability.value: Founded after a Tepanec succession war (1426–1428). Some conquered cities often rebelled.

eliteConflict.value: Tensions with subject cities, and the rival Tlaxcala, which later allied with the Spanish.

armyAndTech.value: Large armies of warriors (eagle and jaguar orders), with obsidian-edged clubs (macuahuitl) and spear-throwers.

majorWars.value: Founding wars (1427–1428). “Flower Wars” with Tlaxcala. A defeat by the Purépecha (1479). The Spanish conquest (1519–1521).

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Tlaxcala and the Purépecha (Tarascan state), who were never conquered.

inventions.value: Chinampa floating-garden farming, causeways and aqueducts serving Tenochtitlan.

scienceEducation.value: Schools for all boys (by class). Calendars and pictographic codices.

openness.value: Absorbed earlier Toltec and Mesoamerican traditions.

religion.value: Aztec religion with Huitzilopochtli as the imperial patron god. Large-scale human sacrifice at the Templo Mayor.

languageWriting.value: Classical Nahuatl (a common language for the region), written in pictographic codices.

artsArchitecture.value: The Templo Mayor, the Sun Stone, featherwork and poetry (Nezahualcoyotl).

socialStructure.value: Nobles, commoners, merchants (pochteca), serfs and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Mexica identity tied to the patron god Huitzilopochtli and the founding of Tenochtitlan. Mexico’s flag shows the founding legend.

neighbours.value: Tlaxcala, the Purépecha, the Mixtecs, the Zapotecs and the Maya.

ideasReligions.value: Its language, Nahuatl, spread widely and gave words to English (e.g. chocolate, tomato).

colonisation.value: A conquering tribute empire. It was itself conquered by Spain (with large Indigenous allied armies) in 1521.

riseSignals.value: The Triple Alliance victory over Azcapotzalco (1428), followed by rapid expansion through tribute.

peakPeriod.value: The reigns of Ahuitzotl and Moctezuma II (c. 1486–1519).

declineSignals.value: Resentment among subject peoples, Spanish arrival with Indigenous allies, and the smallpox epidemic of 1520.

outcome.value: Conquest. Tenochtitlan fell to Cortés and his allies on 13 August 1521. Mexico City was built on its ruins.

sources.value: Codices, Spanish chroniclers (Sahagún, Bernal Díaz), and archaeology. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Smith (2012).

overallCertainty.value: Moderate. Population and sacrifice numbers are debated. Some dates differ (the alliance in 1428 or 1430).
